title: Boulangère potatoes
subtitle: Layered potatoes baked slow in stock
excerpt: Thin potato slices layered with onion and thyme, baked slowly in chicken stock until golden and tender. The classic French gratin that cooks under a roasting joint, absorbing the dripping as it goes.
sourceNotes: Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), classic French kitchen reference for potato gratin methods. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136, layered potato bake with stock as a side for roasts.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble the gratin up to 24 hours ahead, cover, and refrigerate. Add 15 minutes to the bake time from cold.

glossaryTerms.definition: A style of cooking where vegetables, usually potatoes, are baked in stock rather than cream; the name comes from the French baker's oven, where these dishes were traditionally cooked.

content.text: are thinly sliced potatoes baked in stock with onion and thyme until the stock is absorbed and the top turns golden. Unlike a cream gratin, they are light and clean-flavoured, which makes them the natural partner for rich roasts.

The dish takes its name from the French village baker's oven, where households would carry their potato dishes to cook in the cooling oven after the bread came out. Cook them under a leg of lamb or a pork joint and the dripping falls into the tin and flavours every layer.

items.prepNote: waxy variety such as Maris Piper or Desiree

content.text: Use a mandoline or a steady hand with a sharp knife to slice the potatoes to about 3 mm. Even slices matter: thick patches stay hard while thin patches dissolve. A rectangular tin roughly 30 cm × 20 cm gives you good layers for six people.
Heat the oven to 180°C fan (200°C conventional). Rub the tin generously with half the butter.
Peel and slice the potatoes to about 3 mm. Keep them in cold water as you go to stop them browning, then drain and pat dry before layering.

Arrange a layer of potato slices across the base, overlapping slightly. Scatter over some sliced onion, a little garlic, and a few thyme leaves. Season with salt and pepper. Repeat until you have used all the potato and onion, finishing with a neat overlapping top layer of potato.
Pour the hot stock over the layers slowly, letting it settle through. The stock should come about three-quarters of the way up the tin. Dot the remaining butter across the top.

Bake for 90 minutes, uncovered. The top should be golden and the stock fully absorbed. Press the surface gently with a palette knife at the 70-minute mark; if it still feels very wet, keep going. If the top browns before the stock is absorbed, cover loosely with foil and continue.
Rest for 10 minutes before serving. The potatoes firm up slightly as they cool and are much easier to portion.

items.symptom: The potatoes are still hard after 90 minutes
items.cause: The slices were too thick or the stock was cold when poured
items.fix: Cover with foil and give them another 20 minutes. Next time, make sure the stock is hot and slices are no more than 3 mm.

items.symptom: The top is browning but the bottom is still swimming in stock
items.cause: Too much stock was added or the tin was too shallow
items.fix: Cover with foil and reduce the oven to 160°C for the remaining time. The stock will continue to absorb.

items.symptom: The layers have collapsed into a mash
items.cause: A floury potato variety was used, such as King Edward, which breaks down in liquid
items.fix: Use a waxy variety like Maris Piper next time. The flesh holds its shape in stock.
Season each layer generously. The stock itself carries little seasoning so the potato layers need salt at every stage.

content.text: Boulangère potatoes sit alongside the great French kitchen repertoire of side dishes that convert a humble ingredient into something worth the oven space. In restaurants they appear under a rack of lamb or a shoulder of pork; at home they are the sensible choice when cream gratin would make the plate too rich. The leftovers reheat well in a hot oven for 15 minutes, the crust crisping back up.
A vegan version works with vegetable stock and olive oil in place of butter. The flavour is sharper without the butter but entirely good, especially alongside roasted vegetables.
